name: Pɛrɛ (Tignère)
overview: In the majority in their area, the Pɛrɛ live with the Mboum, Hausa, Gbaya and Fulani, whose languages they often speak. Coming from Gañe in Nigeria via Gɛŋfəlabo and Almé, they have matrilineal kinship, a chief and kings, and celebrate the mburi in March to call down blessing. Farming, trade and varied crafts provide their living.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority and largely indigenous group, integrated with the Mboum, Hausa, Gbaya and Fulani; Fulfulde and Mboum are also spoken there.
Pɛrɛ is also spoken in Nigeria.
Marriages within and outside the group; it is mostly women who marry outside, which was not done in the past.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land that belongs to them; there they erect the ɲàŋgòlí, an object they make and before which they pray.
Having come from Gañe (Nigeria), they passed through Gɛŋfəlabo and Almé, with whom they still share the same culture.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A traditional chief and kings; age and elders are respected.
The chief, his notables and the whole community decide by consensus at the chiefdom.
Anyone can talk freely, including unmarried people and in-laws; the wife does not look her husband in the eye, a rule now optional under the influence of Islam.
The former specialised roles (gravediggers, mourners) have disappeared.
Historical grudges persist in tradition, but fade before the law.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Matrilineal kinship; the wife in principle joins her husband.
A boy is considered a man from 17 and marries around 20-21, after building his hut; the woman formerly married from 19.
Steps: marriage proposal, engagement, bride price.
Formerly, the bride price consisted of a hoe and wood; today, of a sum agreed between the families and kola nuts in three lots, which represent the father's prayer and the marriage certificate.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The mburi, in March, brings the whole community together for blessings; the elders honour the ancestors at their graves, in the bush, when a difficulty arises.
Mbɛ̀làɲá, a mountain behind the village, was the place where a large animal was laid as an offering to find out whether one was at peace with God.
Birth is a gift from God; death, God taking back what he gave. Communicating with the dead is disapproved of.
Taboos: incest, insulting an elder. The thief repays, the insulter pays a fine, the murderer was beaten and isolated.
Traditional healers consult the earth, the rosary, the stick and the cowries.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, trade, crafts, wood cutting, odd jobs, associations. Women: farming, trade, associations.
The land belongs to the chief, who allocates the plots.
Ancestral crafts: beds, chairs, clothing and hats, hoes and machetes, for use and for sale.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The pàssí, a large garment with a thousand pleats, and the dʒɔ́nta, similar to the boubou; gùdɛ̀l lépí, a woven covering garment; wrappers, and today skirts and trousers.
People turn to both kinds of medicine; the traditional one remains alive.
Beauty: the helpful, welcoming, polite man, able to solve problems; the hard-working, well-groomed woman and good manager.
Courtship: the man offers gifts and shows he is serious; the woman is respectful, patient and looks after the house.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: kɔ́n (tam-tam), vàm (tam-tam and whistling gourd), oɭáŋdáŋ.
The vàm is danced especially in times of misfortune; the kɔ́n in any circumstance.
The millet harvest festival gave thanks to God; today Ramadan, Tabaski, Easter and New Year are celebrated.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The name of the group is said to have been given by a German missionary.
Food, clothing and beliefs bring the Pɛrɛ closer to the Mboum, the Fulani and the Massa.

sections.title: The names
items: Terms: híbɔ̀ktɔ̀ or hibɔɛ̀ (the chief), jiptó (the man), ɗara (elder sister), ɲále (the woman), ɲalábò (twins).
The name is given at a rite on the seventh day, according to the circumstances; it does not change.
Real names are rarely used: pseudonyms and nicknames dominate, and the royal court assigns some.

lessons.title: Who are the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.langText: NB : il n’y a pas assez de toponyme en pɛ᷅rɛ᷇. Les toponymes sont majoritairement fulfulbe.

lessons.competence: Introduce the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority and largely indigenous group, integrated with the Mboum, Haoussa, Gbaya and Fulani; fulfulde and Mboum are also spoken there. • Pɛrɛ is also spoken in Nigeria. • Marriages within and outside the group; it is mainly women who marry outside, which was not done in the past. • Ancestral land that belongs to them; they erect the ɲàŋgòlí there, an object they make and before which they pray. • Having come from Gañe (Nigeria), they passed through Gɛŋfəlabo and Almé, with which they still share the same culture.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their area, the Pɛrɛ live with the Mboum, Hausa, Gbaya and Fulani, whose languages they often speak. Coming from Gañe in Nigeria via Gɛŋfəlabo and Almé, they have matrilineal kinship, a chief and kings, and celebrate the mburi in March to call down blessing. Farming, trade and varied crafts provide their living.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: maize, banana, yam, beans, gùrká (dry season), sorrel and baobab. • Drinks: hòreʤam, gbàta, bil-bil, porridge. • Men: farming, trade, crafts, woodcutting, odd jobs, associations. Women: farming, trade, associations.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Pɛrɛ (Tignère) mainly eat maize, banana, yam, beans. Traditional drinks: hòreʤam, gbàta, bil-bil. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

activities.instruction: What has changed in marriage today?

student.memo: Steps: marriage proposal, engagement, bride price. Formerly, the bride price consisted of a hoe and wood; today, of a sum agreed between the families and cola in three lots, which represent the father's prayer and the marriage certificate.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Pɛrɛ (Tignère) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Pɛrɛ (Tignère) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: kɔ́n (tam-tam), vàm (tam-tam and whistling gourd), oɭáŋdáŋ. • The vàm is danced mainly in times of misfortune; the kɔ́n on any occasion. • The millet harvest festival used to thank God; today people celebrate Ramadan, Tabaski, Easter and New Year.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), traditional dances (vàm, kɔ́n) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, whistling gourd. Festival(s): mburi, millet harvest festival.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Pɛrɛ (Tignère) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), traditional dances (vàm, kɔ́n) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, whistling gourd. Festival(s): mburi, millet harvest festival.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Pɛrɛ (Tignère). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Pɛrɛ (Tignère). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, trade, crafts, woodcutting, odd jobs, associations. Women: farming, trade, associations. • Land belongs to the chief, who allocates the plots. • Ancestral crafts: beds, chairs, clothes and hats, hoes and machetes, for use and for sale.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, trade, crafts, wood cutting, odd jobs, associations. Women: farming, trade, associations. Land belongs to the chief, who allocates plots.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The mburi, in March, brings the whole community together for blessings; the elders honour the ancestors at their graves, in the bush, when a difficulty arises. • Mbɛ̀làɲá, a mountain behind the village, was the place where a large animal was left as an offering to find out whether one was at peace with God. • Birth is a gift from God; death is God taking back what he gave. Communicating with the dead is disapproved of. • Taboos: incest, insulting an elder. The thief repays, the insulter pays a fine, the murderer was flogged and isolated. • Traditional healers consult the earth, the rosary, the stick and the cowries.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The mburi, in March, brings the whole community together for blessings; the elders honour the ancestors at their graves, in the bush, when a difficulty arises. Mbɛ̀làɲá, a mountain behind the village, was the place where a large animal was laid as an offering to find out whether one was at peace with God.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Pɛrɛ
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Pɛrɛ (Tignère) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Pɛrɛ (Tignère) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Pɛrɛ (Tignère) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Pɛrɛ. • Greetings: mûdo᷇ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); A᷅lu᷇rɛ᷇ = morning greeting (one person); Vo᷇du᷇rɛ᷇ = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Də᷇, Iro᷇, Tə᷅ɳrə᷇, Na᷅rə᷇, Nu᷅nə᷇. • Real names are rarely used: pseudonyms and nicknames predominate, and the royal court assigns them. • The name of the group is said to have been given by a German missionary.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Pɛrɛ are the first steps towards communicating with the Pɛrɛ (Tignère). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
